object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account; everything hangs off it. Identified by account number.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six digit sequential identifier for an account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a certain amount on a certain cycle for a certain product/plan.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Unique generated identifier for a subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product sold by the company, identified by product code.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a product.

source_references.excerpt: We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that generates the invoice line; says what the customer pays and how often. Identified by plan code.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a price plan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: What the customer gets -- the feature bundle (seats, API, SSO). Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: Name of a feature bundle, e.g. Starter, Professional, Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription starts; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; optional, present for fixed-term subscriptions or after cancellation.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The billing cycle of a subscription: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The status of a subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

object_types.name: PausedFlag
object_types.definition: A separate boolean flag indicating a subscription is paused, distinct from status but overlapping in behaviour.

source_references.excerpt: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with effective date and requester; the subscription's current plan is derived from change history.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date... It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.

source_references.excerpt: It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: MRR
object_types.definition: Monthly recurring revenue; derived from the price plan price normalised to a month and the billing period, not stored.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month.

ambiguities.description: The word 'plan' is used for at least three different concepts: the billing artefact (PricePlan), the feature bundle (FeatureBundle), and the sales-negotiated deal mentioned by Tom. The sales-negotiated 'deal' concept was explicitly deferred to another meeting and is not modeled here. Confirm whether it needs to be captured separately in a future session.

source_references.excerpt: So we've got two things both called plan... the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: PausedFlag overlaps confusingly with SubscriptionStatus (a paused subscription may still be queried as 'active'). It is unclear whether Paused should be integrated into the status enumeration or kept as an independent flag with defined interaction rules with each status value.

source_references.excerpt: It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The current PricePlan on Subscription is denormalized/derived from the PlanChange history, yet it is also stored as a field and treated as authoritative unless it disagrees with history (in which case history wins). This creates ambiguity about whether 'Subscription belongs to PricePlan' should be modeled as a stored fact (as done here) or purely derived from the last PlanChange by effective date -- the transcript indicates both views were held by different stakeholders.

source_references.excerpt: No, Sam, it does have a current plan field... And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: The commercial policy for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked by the facilitator. No constraint or fact type for refunds/credits has been modeled since none currently exists in the system, but this is a known gap that needs resolution by finance/legal.

source_references.excerpt: What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided... it will not invent a refund concept that doesn't exist.

ambiguities.description: A fourth product is 'in discovery' and not yet defined; the ProductCode value constraint (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) may need to be revisited when it launches. Flagging in case the value constraint should not be treated as permanently fixed.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Account identity treats a returning company as a brand-new account (new account number), losing historical continuity from a product perspective. It is unclear whether the model should also track a company/organization concept distinct from Account to preserve cross-account history, or whether this is explicitly out of scope.

source_references.excerpt: If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting... It drives finance the other way.

ambiguities.description: Manual refund credits (the four goodwill refunds mentioned) exist outside the subscription model as ad hoc actions; it's unclear if these should be captured as a fact type (e.g., a Credit or Refund entity) for audit/reporting purposes, since Sam indicated a need to classify them as contra-revenue or refund liability.

source_references.excerpt: Four times in a quarter isn't goodwill, it's a policy nobody's written down... I need to know whether to treat those as contra-revenue or as a refund liability.
